claims.source: Gene ontology analysis revealed that the majority of downregulated genes were implicated in processes relevant to nervous system development, including neuron projections and dendritic and synapse development (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: ALCAM, Edil3, cdh9, Ptprt, Lsamp and Negr1 are highly and specifically expressed in the phrenic motor column at e12.5.
claims.source: We found that ALCAM, Edil3, cdh9, Ptprt, Lsamp and Negr1 were highly and specifically expressed in the PMC at e12.5 (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: ALCAM, Edil3, cdh9, Ptprt, Lsamp and Negr1 require Hox5 proteins for their expression.
claims.source: We further found that these phrenic-specific CAMs require Hox5 proteins for their expression, as they were downregulated in Hox5MNΔ; Bax-/- mice (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing downregulation in mutant mice shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Ptprt and Lsamp are novel phrenic motor column genes.
claims.source: A subset of these CAMs were previously established as phrenic-specific markers (ALCAM, Edil3, cdh9 and Negr1), while our analysis also identified novel PMC genes (Ptprt and Lsamp) (Machado et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq and in situ hybridization data, with citation to previous work (Machado et al., 2014) for comparison.

claims.claim: Hox5 proteins regulate phrenic motor column clustering and position through controlling the expression of a network of downstream cell adhesion molecules.
claims.source: Our results suggest that Hox5 proteins regulate PMC clustering and position through controlling the expression of a network of downstream cell adhesion molecules.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed downregulation of cell adhesion molecules in mutant mice and the clustering defects.

claims.claim: Cadherins 2, 6, 9, 10, 11 and 22 are expressed in the phrenic motor column at e13.5.
claims.source: We performed in situ hybridization for all type I and type II cadherins and found that cdh2, 6, 9, 10, 11 and 22 were expressed in the PMC at e13.5, while the rest of the family members were either expressed in other MN subtypes or not found in the spinal cord (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c.

claims.claim: All phrenic motor column cadherins are uniformly expressed in the majority of phrenic motor neurons (>90%) at e13.5.
claims.source: We found that all PMC cadherins were uniformly expressed in the majority of phrenic MNs (>90%) at e13.5 (Figure 4b–c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization combined with Scip immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4b–c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: At cervical levels of the spinal cord, cadherin 9 and 10 expression is restricted to phrenic motor neurons.
claims.source: At cervical levels of the spinal cord, cdh9 and 10 expression appears to be restricted to phrenic MNs, while cdh2, 6, 11 and 22 are broadly expressed in all MN populations (Figure 4b–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4b–c.

claims.claim: Cadherins 2, 6, 11 and 22 are broadly expressed in all motor neuron populations at cervical levels of the spinal cord.
claims.source: At cervical levels of the spinal cord, cdh9 and 10 expression appears to be restricted to phrenic MNs, while cdh2, 6, 11 and 22 are broadly expressed in all MN populations (Figure 4b–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4b–c.

claims.claim: β- and γ-catenin are obligate intracellular factors required for cadherin-mediated cell adhesive function.
claims.source: β- and γ-catenin are obligate intracellular factors required for cadherin-mediated cell adhesive function and are necessary for the organization of limb-innervating motor pools (Demireva et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Demireva et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin in motor neurons leads to a marked disorganization and loss of phrenic motor neuron clustering.
claims.source: Joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin, however, and disruption of cadherin signaling, led to a marked disorganization and loss of phrenic MN clustering (Figure 5b–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from βγ-catMNΔ mice shown in Figure 5b–c.

claims.claim: The phrenic motor column clustering index is significantly reduced in βγ-catMNΔ mice at e13.5.
claims.source: We find that the PMC clustering index is significantly reduced in βγ-catMNΔ mice at e13.5 (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of clustering index shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: There is a ~30% reduction in the number of Scip+ motor neurons that settle in the ventral spinal cord in βγ-catMNΔ mice.
claims.source: We also observed a ~30% reduction in the number of Scip+ MNs that settle in the ventral spinal cord in βγ-catMNΔ mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), partly due to the failure of a subset of PMC neurons to migrate away from the midline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: There is a change in dendritic orientation and loss of the dorsal-most dendrites in βγ-catMNΔ mice.
claims.source: Similar to Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice, we found a change in dendritic orientation and loss of the dorsal-most dendrites in βγ-catMNΔ mice (Figure 5d–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by diI tracing data shown in Figure 5d–e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claims.claim: Joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin did not affect phrenic axon growth or guidance.
claims.source: Despite having a striking effect on PMC dendrites, joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin did not affect phrenic axon growth or guidance, as diaphragm innervation appears normal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Hox5 genes control phrenic axon and dendrite development through distinct molecular programs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing normal diaphragm innervation in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Hox5 genes control phrenic axon and dendrite development through distinct molecular programs.
claims.source: Despite having a striking effect on PMC dendrites, joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin did not affect phrenic axon growth or guidance, as diaphragm innervation appears normal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Hox5 genes control phrenic axon and dendrite development through distinct molecular programs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of catenin deletion on dendrites versus axons.

claims.claim: Cadherins are required in phrenic motor neurons downstream of Hox5 genes for proper clustering and dendritic orientation.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that cadherins are required in phrenic MNs downstream of Hox5 genes for proper clustering and dendritic orientation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar phenotypes observed in Hox5 mutants and catenin mutants.

claims.claim: No significant changes in phrenic nerve burst frequency, rhythmicity, or duration were observed in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice at P4.
claims.source: Despite the changes in PMC clustering and dendritic topography, no significant changes in phrenic nerve burst frequency, rhythmicity, or duration were observed in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice (Figure 6b–c), indicating that the brainstem circuits that drive inspiratory bursts, located within the pre-Bötzinger complex, are intact and able to transmit excitatory drive to phrenic MNs via the rVRG.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data shown in Figure 6b–c.

claims.claim: The brainstem circuits that drive inspiratory bursts are intact in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: Despite the changes in PMC clustering and dendritic topography, no significant changes in phrenic nerve burst frequency, rhythmicity, or duration were observed in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice (Figure 6b–c), indicating that the brainstem circuits that drive inspiratory bursts, located within the pre-Bötzinger complex, are intact and able to transmit excitatory drive to phrenic MNs via the rVRG.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal burst frequency and rhythmicity in mutant mice.

claims.claim: The phrenic firing pattern within inspiratory bursts is dramatically altered in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: Remarkably, this pattern in inspiratory bursts is abolished in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Inspiratory bursts in control mice are composed of periods of activity interspersed with silent periods with no unit activity.
claims.source: We found that MN bursts from control (Hoxa5 flox/flox; Hoxc5+/-) mice exhibited a highly reproducible firing pattern, with inspiratory bursts comprised of periods of activity interspersed with periods with no unit activity (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Periods of activity in control mice are dominated by large amplitude rhythmic oscillations that occur at approximately 30 Hz.
claims.source: In addition, periods of activity are dominated by large amplitude rhythmic oscillations that occur at approximately 30 Hz (Figure 6d), generated by the summations of multiple phrenic MN units firing in the same temporal pattern.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: The 30 Hz oscillations in phrenic motor neuron firing are matched to the fusion frequency of the diaphragm muscle.
claims.source: Interestingly, these 30 Hz oscillations are matched to the fusion frequency of the diaphragm muscle, which is the frequency of firing at which the diaphragm is tonically and maximally contracted (Martin-Caraballo et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Martin-Caraballo et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Patterned firing of phrenic motor neurons close to the fusion frequency promotes highly efficient diaphragm contraction.
claims.source: Thus, patterned firing of phrenic MNs close to the fusion frequency promotes highly efficient diaphragm contraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the match between firing frequency and muscle fusion frequency.

claims.claim: Inspiratory bursts in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice exhibit near continuous firing.
claims.source: Inspiratory bursts exhibit near continuous firing after loss of Hox5 genes, and thus the silent periods within the burst are largely lost (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: The large amplitude rhythmic 30 Hz activity is eliminated in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: In addition, the large amplitude rhythmic 30 Hz activity was eliminated, suggesting that the firing of phrenic MNs in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice is no longer constrained to occur at specific times but is instead distributed throughout the burst, thus reducing the compound action potentials seen in control mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data and power spectrum analysis.

claims.claim: Power spectrum analysis shows a decrease in 30 Hz activity with a concomitant broad spectrum increase in higher frequencies in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: Power spectrum analysis to resolve the recording into its component frequencies indicated a decrease in 30 Hz activity with a concomitant broad spectrum increase in higher frequencies (Figure 6f–g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 6f–g.

claims.claim: Firing of phrenic motor neurons in an unpatterned manner increases the risk of phrenic motor neuron adaptation, diaphragm muscle fatigue, and respiratory failure.
claims.source: Importantly, firing of phrenic MNs in an unpatterned manner that does not correlate with the diaphragm fusion frequency provides no additional contractile benefit, and in fact may increase the risk of phrenic MN adaptation, diaphragm muscle fatigue, and respiratory failure (Martin-Caraballo et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Martin-Caraballo et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Bursts from Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice at the time of birth (P0) display a similar change in motor output as at P4.
claims.source: In addition, bursts from Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice at the time of birth (P0) display a similar change in motor output (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–d), suggesting that Hox5 genes function during embryonic development to shape phrenic MN activity at birth.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data at P0 shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–d.

claims.claim: Hox5 genes function during embryonic development to shape phrenic motor neuron activity at birth.
claims.source: In addition, bursts from Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice at the time of birth (P0) display a similar change in motor output (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–d), suggesting that Hox5 genes function during embryonic development to shape phrenic MN activity at birth.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of altered firing patterns at birth.

claims.claim: Hox5-dependent transcriptional programs are required for shaping the pattern of phrenic motor neuron output.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that Hox5-dependent transcriptional programs are required for shaping the pattern of phrenic MN output and confining firing to frequency oscillations that promote efficient diaphragm contraction while preventing muscle failure.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed changes in firing patterns in mutant mice.

claims.claim: Phrenic motor neuron firing pattern and synchronicity are thought to be generated in part by inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: Phrenic MN firing pattern and synchronicity are thought to be generated in part by inhibitory synaptic transmission that modulates firing in response to excitatory drive (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Marchenko and Rogers, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Marchenko and Rogers, 2009).

claims.claim: Injection of picrotoxin and strychnine in control mice results in a firing pattern indistinguishable from that seen in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: Injection of picrotoxin and strychnine in control mice resulted in a firing pattern indistinguishable from that seen in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data after disinhibition shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Disinhibited control phrenic motor neurons fire throughout the burst with reduced periods of no activity.
claims.source: Disinhibited control phrenic MNs fired throughout the burst with reduced periods of no activity (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data after disinhibition shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Power spectra analysis of disinhibited control mice reveals a decrease in 30 Hz activity with a concomitant broad increase in high frequency activity.
claims.source: Power spectra analysis revealed a decrease in 30 Hz activity with a concomitant broad increase in high frequency activity (Figure 7c–d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by power spectrum analysis after disinhibition shown in Figure 7c–d.

claims.claim: Picrotoxin and strychnine injections into Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice had little effect on phrenic motor neuron firing.
claims.source: Picrotoxin and strychnine injections into Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice had little effect on phrenic MN firing (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phrenic nerve recording data after disinhibition shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice have lost the inhibitory synaptic transmission which is important for generating patterned phrenic motor neuron firing.
claims.source: The ability to convert the firing pattern of control mice into one similar to Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice by disinhibition locally on the PMC, and the fact that disinhibition had little effect on Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het phrenic MN firing, implies that Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice have lost the inhibitory synaptic transmission which is important for generating this pattern.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the disinhibition experiments showing similar firing patterns.

claims.claim: Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice exhibit a 20% reduction in inhibitory synapse number on phrenic motor neurons compared to control.
claims.source: Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice exhibited a 20% reduction in inhibitory synapse number as compared to control (Figure 7g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by synaptic puncta quantitation shown in Figure 7g.

claims.claim: Functional phrenic motor neuron output is altered in the absence of Hox5 genes, likely due to loss of a subset of inhibitory inputs.
claims.source: Our results show that functional phrenic MN output is altered in the absence of Hox5 genes, likely due to loss of a subset of inhibitory inputs that act to pattern motor output.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the disinhibition experiments and synaptic puncta quantitation.

claims.claim: Hox5-dependent transcriptional programs shape the pattern of respiratory output by establishing inhibitory inputs onto phrenic motor neurons.
claims.source: Together, our data support a model where Hox5-dependent transcriptional programs shape the pattern of respiratory output by establishing inhibitory inputs onto phrenic MNs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of electrophysiology, disinhibition experiments, and synaptic analysis.

claims.claim: The establishment of phrenic motor neuron identity relies on the intersection of transcription factor-based programs acting along the dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes of the spinal cord during development.
claims.source: The establishment of phrenic motor neuron (MN) identity relies on the intersection of transcription factor-based programs acting along the dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes of the spinal cord during development (Chaimowicz et al., 2019; Edmond et al., 2017; Philippidou et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chaimowicz et al., 2019; Edmond et al., 2017; Philippidou et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Fetal contractions of the diaphragm muscle are essential for lung and diaphragm development.
claims.source: Fetal contractions of the diaphragm muscle are essential for lung and diaphragm development and defects in these contractions result in lung hypoplasia and central sleep apneas (Harding, 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Harding, 1997).

claims.claim: Coupling of phrenic motor neurons through gap junctions is critical to maintain early diaphragm contractions during embryonic stages.
claims.source: Because inspiratory drive is relatively weak during embryonic stages, coupling of phrenic MNs through gap junctions is critical to maintain early diaphragm contractions (Greer and Funk, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Greer and Funk, 2005).

claims.claim: Phrenic motor neurons lack monosynaptic sensory input from Ia proprioceptive afferents.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike the majority of MNs in the spinal cord, phrenic MNs appear to lack monosynaptic sensory input from Ia proprioceptive afferents and extensive inputs from spinal cord interneurons (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The majority of phrenic motor neuron monosynaptic inputs (~70%) are derived from the rostral Ventral Respiratory Group (rVRG).
claims.source: Instead, the majority of their monosynaptic inputs (~70%) are derived from the rostral Ventral Respiratory Group (rVRG), a group of mostly glutamatergic neurons in the brainstem that transmit the excitatory drive to activate MNs in a rhythmic pattern generated in the pre-Bötzinger complex (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Inspiratory-phase inhibitory inputs onto phrenic motor neurons rapidly modulate motor neuron excitability to act as a gain control for motor output.
claims.source: Inspiratory-phase inhibitory inputs onto phrenic MNs rapidly modulate MN excitability to act as a gain control for motor output and control motor neuron synchronization within respiratory bursts (Parkis et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Parkis et al., 1999).

claims.claim: Synchronous inspiratory motor neuron firing on a short time scale enhances inspiratory muscle activation.
claims.source: Synchronous inspiratory MN firing on a short time scale is thought to enhance inspiratory muscle activation, thus ensuring robust and efficient breathing (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001).

claims.claim: Loss of Hox5 genes renders mice particularly vulnerable to respiratory dysfunction in the first two weeks of life.
claims.source: Hox5 loss renders mice particularly vulnerable to respiratory dysfunction in the first two weeks of life, suggesting that Hox5 mutations may contribute to early life respiratory conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal analysis of respiratory dysfunction showing severe ventilation deficits in the first two weeks.

claims.claim: Hox5 mutations may contribute to early life respiratory conditions.
claims.source: Hox5 loss renders mice particularly vulnerable to respiratory dysfunction in the first two weeks of life, suggesting that Hox5 mutations may contribute to early life respiratory conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed vulnerability to respiratory dysfunction in mutant mice.

claims.claim: Motor neuron-specific deletion of Hox5 genes results in a selective loss of inhibitory inputs to phrenic motor column neurons.
claims.source: MN-specific deletion of Hox5 genes results in a selective loss of inhibitory inputs to PMC neurons and a dramatic change in the activation pattern of phrenic MNs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by disinhibition experiments and synaptic puncta quantitation.

claims.claim: Hox5 transcription factors determine phrenic motor neuron topography and connectivity to generate robust breathing behaviors.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that Hox5 transcription factors determine phrenic MN topography and connectivity to generate robust breathing behaviors.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing effects on clustering, dendritic orientation, inhibitory inputs, and breathing behavior.

claims.claim: The ability to overcome hypercapnic and hypoxic conditions is particularly important during perinatal stages.
claims.source: Notably, the ability to overcome hypercapnic and hypoxic conditions is particularly important during perinatal stages, as a compromised response to respiratory insults could increase susceptibility to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) (Kinney et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kinney et al., 2009).

claims.claim: A compromised response to respiratory insults could increase susceptibility to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
claims.source: Notably, the ability to overcome hypercapnic and hypoxic conditions is particularly important during perinatal stages, as a compromised response to respiratory insults could increase susceptibility to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) (Kinney et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kinney et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Phrenic motor neuron clustering likely serves a dual function during development, enabling both electrical coupling and premotor targeting.
claims.source: Therefore, phrenic MN clustering likely serves a dual function during development, enabling both electrical coupling and premotor targeting.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the known functions of clustering in electrical coupling and the stereotypical organization that could facilitate targeting.

claims.claim: Phrenic motor neuron dendrites form tightly fasciculated bundles that adopt a distinct ventromedial and dorsolateral orientation during development.
claims.source: Phrenic MN dendrites form tightly fasciculated bundles that adopt a distinct ventromedial and dorsolateral orientation during development (Allan and Greer, 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Allan and Greer, 1997).

claims.claim: By late embryonic stages (e18.5), phrenic dendrites are restricted to the ipsilateral side and rarely cross the midline.
claims.source: By late embryonic stages (e18.5), phrenic dendrites are restricted to the ipsilateral side and rarely cross the midline.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from diI tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Expression of single or a small subset of cadherins may be insufficient to endow phrenic motor column neurons with a unique identity for self-recognition.
claims.source: Expression of single or a small subset of cadherins may be insufficient to endow PMC neurons with a unique identity for self-recognition, and multiple cadherin expression might be necessary for their segregation from limb-innervating and axial MNs found at the same levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of multiple cadherin expression in phrenic motor neurons.

claims.claim: Phrenic motor column cadherins belong to all three specificity groups identified on the basis of their heterophilic interactions.
claims.source: PMC cadherins belong to all three specificity groups identified recently on the basis of their heterophilic interactions, further restricting the likelihood that PMC neurons will interact with other MN populations through heterophilic interactions between cadherins of the same subgroup (Brasch et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Brasch et al., 2018) and the observed cadherin expression pattern.

claims.claim: N-cadherin function is required for clustering of all motor neuron populations.
claims.source: While the function of the type I cadherin, N-cadherin is required for clustering of all MN populations, additional type II cadherin divergent expression among MN populations may be required for specific MN subtype clustering (Dewitz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Dewitz et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Additional type II cadherin divergent expression among motor neuron populations may be required for specific motor neuron subtype clustering.
claims.source: While the function of the type I cadherin, N-cadherin is required for clustering of all MN populations, additional type II cadherin divergent expression among MN populations may be required for specific MN subtype clustering (Dewitz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Dewitz et al., 2019).

claims.claim: A subpopulation of neurons in the pre-Bötzinger complex expresses cadherin 9.
claims.source: Interestingly, a subpopulation of neurons in the pre-Bötzinger complex also expresses cdh9, which could indicate a broad role for cadherins is establishing synaptic connectivity throughout respiratory circuits (Yackle et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Yackle et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Cadherins may have a broad role in establishing synaptic connectivity throughout respiratory circuits.
claims.source: Interestingly, a subpopulation of neurons in the pre-Bötzinger complex also expresses cdh9, which could indicate a broad role for cadherins is establishing synaptic connectivity throughout respiratory circuits (Yackle et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of cadherin 9 expression in pre-Bötzinger complex neurons.

claims.claim: Motor neuron identity is emerging as a critical determinant of motor neuron connectivity.
claims.source: MN identity, established by early transcriptional programs, is emerging as a critical determinant of MN connectivity (Dasen, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Dasen, 2017).

claims.claim: The correct positioning of motor neurons is critical for their targeting by sensory axons in sensory-motor circuits.
claims.source: In sensory-motor circuits, the correct positioning of MNs appears to be critical for their targeting by sensory axons (Sürmeli et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Sürmeli et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Spatial features of the motor neuron dendritic tree can act as a determinant of connectivity with sensory neurons.
claims.source: In addition, it has recently been reported that spatial features of the MN dendritic tree, such as the angle of interaction with approaching axons, can also act as a determinant of their connectivity with sensory neurons (Balaskas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Balaskas et al., 2019).

claims.claim: In the retina, cadherins control the topography of axonal and dendritic arbors of synaptic partners to place them in close proximity and enable synaptogenesis.
claims.source: In the retina, cadherins control the topography of axonal and dendritic arbors of synaptic partners to place them in close proximity and enable synaptogenesis (Duan et al., 2014; Duan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Duan et al., 2014; Duan et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In the hippocampus, cadherins influence synaptic fidelity and potentiation without overtly affecting cell morphology.
claims.source: In the hippocampus however, cadherins influence synaptic fidelity and potentiation without overtly affecting cell morphology, pointing to position-independent roles in synaptic connectivity (Basu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Basu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Mutations in transcription factors that alter molecular identity but not cell body position dramatically reconfigure motor neuron inputs.
claims.source: Similarly, mutations in transcription factors that alter molecular identity but not cell body position dramatically reconfigure MN inputs, indicating that MN position is unlikely to be the only critical parameter for MN connectivity (Hinckley et al., 2015; Machado et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Hinckley et al., 2015; Machado et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Loss of inhibitory inputs onto phrenic motor column neurons likely results from both positional and molecular changes resulting from motor neuron-specific Hox5 deletion.
claims.source: Loss of inhibitory inputs onto PMC neurons likely results from both positional and molecular changes resulting from MN-specific Hox5 deletion.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed changes in both topography and molecular identity in mutant mice.

claims.claim: Rabies-virus mediated retrograde tracing revealed a population of phrenic motor column-projecting inhibitory neurons within the rostral Ventral Respiratory Group.
claims.source: Rabies-virus mediated retrograde tracing revealed a population of PMC-projecting inhibitory neurons within the rVRG (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Excitatory and inhibitory rostral Ventral Respiratory Group neurons are activated concurrently, such that inhibition is in phase with excitatory inputs generating inspiration.
claims.source: Excitatory and inhibitory rVRG neurons are activated concurrently, such that inhibition is in phase with excitatory inputs generating inspiration (Parkis et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Parkis et al., 1999).

claims.claim: Inspiratory-phase inhibition synchronizes motor neuron output on a short time scale.
claims.source: This inspiratory-phase inhibition synchronizes MN output on a short time scale, and this oscillation frequency is thought to match the frequency that produces maximal muscle force to generate robust diaphragm contractions (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Parkis et al., 2003; Sebe et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Parkis et al., 2003; Sebe et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The oscillation frequency of inspiratory-phase inhibition is thought to match the frequency that produces maximal muscle force to generate robust diaphragm contractions.
claims.source: This inspiratory-phase inhibition synchronizes MN output on a short time scale, and this oscillation frequency is thought to match the frequency that produces maximal muscle force to generate robust diaphragm contractions (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Parkis et al., 2003; Sebe et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Bou-Flores and Berger, 2001; Parkis et al., 2003; Sebe et al., 2006).

claims.claim: There are multiple contributing factors to respiratory dysfunction in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice, including loss of diaphragm innervation, reduction in phrenic motor neuron numbers, and inefficient activation of remaining phrenic motor neurons.
claims.source: There are likely multiple contributing factors to this respiratory dysfunction, including the loss of diaphragm innervation, the reduction in phrenic MN numbers and the inefficient activation of the remaining phrenic MNs due to the loss of electrical coupling and inhibitory inputs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of the study.

claims.claim: At birth, the vast majority of phrenic motor neurons are recruited at rest.
claims.source: At birth, the vast majority of phrenic MNs are recruited at rest, making the impact of phrenic MN loss on tidal volume more pronounced.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about motor unit recruitment in neonates.

claims.claim: As motor units mature, recruitment of a small subset of phrenic motor neurons is sufficient to generate efficient diaphragm contractions.
claims.source: As motor units mature, recruitment of a small subset of phrenic MNs is sufficient to generate efficient diaphragm contractions, partly compensating for phrenic MN loss.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about motor unit maturation, supported by citation (Greer et al., 1999).

claims.claim: Upon a respiratory challenge such as hypercapnia, no additional motor units are available to be recruited in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: However, upon a respiratory challenge such as hypercapnia, no additional motor units are available to be recruited in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice, leading to severe decreases in minute ventilation and compromising the hypercapnia response.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced motor neuron numbers and the observed blunted response to hypercapnia.

claims.claim: The compensation for tidal volume reduction by increasing breathing frequency does not occur until 2 weeks of age in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice.
claims.source: In Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice there is a gradual compensation for tidal volume reduction by increasing breathing frequency at rest. However, this compensation does not occur until 2 weeks of age, likely reflecting the maturation of central chemosensory regions that provide respiratory feedback (Putnam et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of neonatal respiration and a citation to previous work (Putnam et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Hox5 mutations render mice particularly vulnerable to respiratory failure during the first 2 weeks of life.
claims.source: This indicates that Hox5 mutations render mice particularly vulnerable to respiratory failure during the first 2 weeks of life, and consistent with this we observe increased perinatal lethality in Hoxa5MNΔ; c5het mice, reminiscent of SIDS.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal analysis of respiratory dysfunction and observed perinatal lethality.

claims.claim: Gene variants causing defects in phrenic motor neuron connectivity and function may be an alternative risk factor for neonatal lethality.
claims.source: While much attention has been focused on identifying deleterious genetic variants that impair CO2-sensing populations, such as serotonergic neurons, as causal to SIDS, another possibility is that gene variants causing defects in phrenic MN connectivity and function may be an alternative risk factor for neonatal lethality (Kinney et al., 2009; Rand et al., 2013; Van Norstrand and Ackerman, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed respiratory dysfunction and perinatal lethality in mutant mice, with citations to previous work on SIDS (Kinney et al., 2009; Rand et al., 2013; Van Norstrand and Ackerman, 2010).

claims.claim: Mutations in Hox5 transcription factors or downstream cell adhesion molecules may lead to respiratory dysfunction in humans and be a genetic risk factor for SIDS.
claims.source: As GWAS studies are becoming increasingly common, they may in the future reveal that mutations in Hox5 transcription factors, or downstream cell adhesion molecules, also lead to respiratory dysfunction in humans and are a genetic risk factor for SIDS.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from mouse studies to potential human implications.

results.result: Hoxa5MNΔ;c5het mice exhibit respiratory dysfunction characterized by reduced tidal volume, compensatory increased breathing frequency, and impaired response to hypercapnia. Neonatal mice show severe ventilation deficits in the first two weeks of life with ~50% perinatal lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C13 provide converging evidence from plethysmography experiments showing consistent respiratory deficits. The data demonstrate reduced tidal volume (C5, C10), compensatory frequency increases (C6, C11), maintained minute ventilation at rest (C7), impaired hypercapnic response (C8-C9), and temporal vulnerability in early postnatal life (C10-C13). The measurements are quantified with appropriate controls and statistical significance is indicated.

results.result: Hox5 genes control phrenic motor neuron clustering and dendritic topography. Loss of Hox5 genes results in disorganized PMC clustering, loss of dorsolateral dendrites, increased medial dendrites, and aberrant midline crossing.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 are supported by diI tracing experiments with quantitative clustering index measurements (C17) and dendritic orientation analysis (C19-C21). The data show consistent phenotypes across multiple embryos with statistical significance. The inference that Hox5 genes control these features (C18, C22) is reasonable given the loss-of-function phenotype, though causality is correlative.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis identified 837 differentially expressed genes in Hox5 mutants, including downregulation of phrenic-specific cell adhesion molecules (ALCAM, Edil3, cdh9, Ptprt, Lsamp, Negr1) that are regulated by Hox5 proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 are supported by RNA-seq data (C23-C24) validated by in situ hybridization (C25-C26). The identification of novel PMC genes Ptprt and Lsamp (C27) is appropriately contextualized with prior work. The inference that Hox5 proteins regulate PMC clustering through CAMs (C28) is reasonable but represents a mechanistic hypothesis requiring further validation beyond correlation.

results.result: A comprehensive cadherin expression analysis identified six cadherins (cdh2, 6, 9, 10, 11, 22) expressed in >90% of phrenic motor neurons at e13.5, with cdh9 and cdh10 showing PMC-restricted expression at cervical levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by systematic in situ hybridization for all type I and II cadherins combined with quantitative fluorescence in situ hybridization. The comprehensive approach and high percentage of expressing neurons (>90%, C30) provide strong evidence for the cadherin code. The spatial restriction of cdh9/10 (C31) versus broad expression of others (C32) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Joint inactivation of β- and γ-catenin in motor neurons disrupts cadherin signaling, leading to PMC disorganization, reduced clustering, altered dendritic orientation, but preserved axon guidance. This demonstrates cadherins act downstream of Hox5 genes to control PMC topography.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 are supported by genetic experiments showing phenocopy of Hox5 mutant phenotypes in β/γ-catenin double mutants. The clustering defects (C34-C35), dendritic changes (C37), and preserved axon guidance (C38) are well-documented. The inference of distinct molecular programs for axons versus dendrites (C39) and downstream cadherin requirement (C40) is reasonable given the phenotypic similarities, though epistasis is not formally demonstrated.

results.result: Hox5 genes shape the pattern of phrenic motor neuron firing within inspiratory bursts. While burst frequency and duration are normal, Hox5 mutants show loss of silent periods, elimination of 30 Hz oscillations, and shift to continuous high-frequency firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C50 are supported by phrenic nerve recordings from brainstem-spinal cord preparations. The preservation of burst frequency/duration (C41-C42) but altered intra-burst pattern (C43-C45, C48-C50) is clearly demonstrated with power spectrum analysis. The quantification of silent periods and frequency distribution provides robust evidence for the firing pattern changes.

results.result: Pharmacological disinhibition with picrotoxin and strychnine converts control firing patterns to match Hox5 mutants, while having minimal effect on mutants. This demonstrates loss of inhibitory synaptic transmission (confirmed by 20% reduction in inhibitory synapses) underlies the altered firing pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 provide strong converging evidence from pharmacology (C56-C59) and anatomy (C61). The disinhibition experiments elegantly demonstrate that loss of inhibition is sufficient to phenocopy the mutant (C56-C58) and that mutants lack this inhibition (C59). The anatomical reduction in inhibitory synapses (C61) provides structural correlate. The mechanistic inference (C60, C62-C63) is well-supported by the combined functional and anatomical data.

results.result: Hox5 mutations render mice vulnerable to respiratory dysfunction particularly in the first two weeks of life, potentially contributing to early life respiratory conditions including SIDS. Multiple factors contribute including reduced innervation, motor neuron loss, and inefficient activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 and C102-C104 are speculative extrapolations to human disease (SIDS) based on mouse phenotypes. While the temporal vulnerability (C71, C101-C102) is well-documented, the connection to SIDS (C72, C103-C104) is hypothetical without human genetic data. The multifactorial nature of respiratory dysfunction (C97, C100) is a reasonable inference but represents interpretation rather than direct demonstration. The speculation about human relevance is appropriately cautious but remains uncertain.

results.result: The altered phrenic motor neuron firing pattern is present at birth (P0), indicating Hox5 genes function during embryonic development to shape motor neuron activity and establish patterned respiratory output.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by electrophysiological recordings at P0 showing similar firing pattern defects as at P4. The presence of the phenotype at birth (C52) supports the inference that Hox5 acts during embryonic development (C53). The conclusion about Hox5-dependent transcriptional programs shaping output (C54) is reasonable given the developmental timing, though direct embryonic manipulation would strengthen causality.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about phrenic motor neuron development, respiratory circuit organization, and the role of cell adhesion molecules in neural connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C15, C64-C70, C75-C78, C86-C91, C93-C96 are appropriately cited to prior literature. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.

results.result: Background claims about cadherin function, muscle physiology, and motor unit recruitment that contextualize the experimental findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C46-C47, C51, C55, C82-C85, C92, C98-C99 provide important physiological and molecular context. The citations to prior work appear appropriate. The connection between 30 Hz firing and muscle fusion frequency (C46-C47) is particularly important for interpreting the functional significance of the firing pattern changes.

results.result: Multiple cadherin expression may be necessary for PMC neuron identity and segregation, with PMC cadherins belonging to all three specificity groups to restrict heterophilic interactions with other motor neuron populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are speculative interpretations of the cadherin expression data. While C81 is supported by citation to cadherin specificity groups (Brasch et al., 2018), the functional significance for PMC segregation (C80) is hypothetical. The expression pattern is consistent with this model but does not directly demonstrate the proposed function. Functional experiments would be needed to test these hypotheses.
